topics.title: Introduction & Functional Classification of Cost
explain: A Cost Sheet is a statement providing detailed cost information classified on a functional basis.
A cost object is any product, service, or cost centre for which costs are measured and accumulated.
Functional classification divides costs according to the business activity for which they are incurred.
The primary functional categories are Production/Manufacturing, Administration, Selling, Distribution, and Research & Development.
topics.example: Wages paid to factory operators are classified under Production Cost, while salaries paid to showroom staff are classified under Selling Cost.
remember: Functional classification groups costs based on the specific business function they support.
mistakes: Confusing functional classification (by activity) with behavioral classification (fixed vs. variable).

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a functional classification of cost?
quiz.why: Variable cost is a classification by cost behavior, not by function.

quiz.q: A traditional cost sheet primarily arranges cost information based on which classification?
quiz.why: Cost sheets conventionally present cost information based on functional classification.

topics.title: Prime Cost and Direct Cost Elements
explain: Prime Cost represents the sum total of all direct costs: Direct Material, Direct Labour, and Direct Expenses.
Direct Material Consumed = Opening Stock + Purchases + Freight Inwards - Closing Stock.
Duties and taxes are added to material cost only if Input Tax Credit (ITC) is NOT available or availed.
Direct Employee (Labour) Cost includes direct wages, incentives, overtime premium, and employer contribution to PF/ESIS.
Direct Expenses are costs traceable to a specific cost object, such as job royalties, specific equipment hire, or custom moulds.

flow.title: Prime Cost Calculation
steps: Add Direct Labour and Employee Benefits

topics.example: Purchasing raw leather, paying freight to bring it to the workshop, and paying wages to shoe cobblers forms the Prime Cost of shoes.
remember: Prime Cost = Direct Material Consumed + Direct Employee Cost + Direct Expenses.
mistakes: Including GST in raw material cost when Input Tax Credit (ITC) is available.

quiz.q: How is Direct Material Consumed calculated in a Cost Sheet?
o: Opening Stock + Purchases + Freight Inwards - Closing Stock
quiz.why: Direct Material Consumed = Opening Stock + Purchases + Freight Inwards - Closing Stock.

quiz.q: Hire charges paid for a specific machine used exclusively for a custom customer order are classified as:
quiz.why: Expenses directly traceable to a specific job or cost object are Direct Expenses.

topics.title: Cost of Production & Factory Overheads
explain: Gross Works Cost is calculated by adding Factory (Works) Overheads to Prime Cost.
Factory Overheads include indirect factory costs like consumable stores, factory supervisor salary, and machine depreciation.
Works Cost / Factory Cost = Gross Works Cost + Opening Work-in-Process (WIP) - Closing WIP.
Cost of Production includes Works Cost, Quality Control cost, process R&D, production-related Admin Overheads, and Primary Packing.
Realizable scrap/waste value is deducted, while primary packing (essential to hold/preserve the product) is added to arrive at Cost of Production.

flow.title: Cost of Production Determination
steps: Add Quality Control and Process R&D

topics.example: Putting milk into plastic pouches is primary packing, which is essential to preserve the product and forms part of Cost of Production.
remember: Cost of Production includes Quality Control, Process R&D, Production Admin Overheads, and Primary Packing.
mistakes: Adding general administrative overheads to Cost of Production instead of Cost of Sales.

quiz.q: Where is the realisable value from the sale of manufacturing scrap deducted in a cost sheet?
quiz.why: Scrap recovery directly reduces the Cost of Production.

quiz.q: Primary packing material essential to hold and preserve a liquid product is included in:
quiz.why: Primary packing is essential for product containment/preservation and forms part of Cost of Production.

topics.title: Cost of Goods Sold and Cost of Sales
explain: Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) = Cost of Production + Opening Finished Goods - Closing Finished Goods.
Cost of Sales (Total Cost) = COGS + General Administration Overheads + Selling Overheads + Secondary Packing + Distribution Overheads.
General Admin Overheads cover corporate office costs like corporate salaries, legal fees, audit fees, and office building depreciation.
Selling Overheads are marketing expenses incurred to secure orders, such as sales commission, advertisement, and market research.
Distribution Overheads are costs incurred in making goods available to customers, including delivery vehicle depreciation and freight out.
Secondary packing enables transport and display (e.g., corrugated cartons for shipping).

flow.title: From Cost of Production to Cost of Sales
steps: Add Secondary Packing and Distribution Overheads

topics.example: Packing 24 juice boxes into a large wooden crate for shipping across states is secondary packing, which goes under Distribution/Cost of Sales.
remember: Cost of Sales = Cost of Goods Sold + General Admin + Selling + Secondary Packing + Distribution Overheads.
mistakes: Valuing closing finished goods inventory at Cost of Sales rather than Cost of Production.

quiz.q: Which inventory adjustment converts Cost of Production into Cost of Goods Sold?
quiz.why: COGS = Cost of Production + Opening Finished Goods - Closing Finished Goods.

quiz.q: Depreciation on delivery vans used for customer order fulfilment is classified under:
quiz.why: Costs related to logistics and delivery vehicles belong to Distribution Overheads.

topics.title: Special Items & Exclusions in Cost Sheet
explain: Abnormal Costs (e.g., pandemic shutdown costs, abnormal idle time) are strictly excluded from Cost of Production.
Subsidies, grants, or incentives received are deducted from the respective cost object.
Penalties, fines, damages, and demurrage are non-cost items and must be completely excluded from the cost sheet.
Interest and Finance Charges on non-equity funds are excluded from Cost of Production and presented separately under Cost of Sales.
GST with available Input Tax Credit (ITC) is excluded from raw material purchase costs.

flow.title: Treatment of Special Items
steps: Present Interest separately under Cost of Sales

topics.example: A traffic fine paid for late delivery is a penalty and is completely excluded from the cost sheet.
remember: Penalties, fines, damages, and abnormal costs never form part of any cost head in a cost sheet.
mistakes: Including interest on bank loans inside Factory Overheads instead of presenting it under Cost of Sales.

quiz.q: How are fines and penalties treated when preparing a Cost Sheet?
o: Excluded entirely from the Cost Sheet
quiz.why: Fines, penalties, and demurrage are non-operating abnormal items and are completely excluded.

quiz.q: Where should Interest and Finance charges be presented in a Cost Statement?
o: As a separate line item of Cost of Sales
quiz.why: Interest and finance charges are presented as a separate item of Cost of Sales.

topics.title: Advantages and Format of Cost Sheet
explain: A Cost Sheet provides both total cost and per-unit cost at every stage of production and sales.
It enables cost comparison across different time periods, processes, or departments.
It helps management in fixing selling prices and preparing accurate estimates for tender quotations.
It aids cost control by highlighting operational inefficiencies and cost overruns.
Unit cost calculations for production costs use 'Units Produced', while selling costs use 'Units Sold'.

flow.title: Standard Cost Sheet Structure
steps: Factory/Works Cost (Prime Cost + Factory Overheads + WIP)
Cost of Production (Works Cost + Quality + R&D + Primary Packing)
Cost of Goods Sold (Cost of Production + Finished Goods)
Cost of Sales (COGS + Admin + Selling & Distribution)
Profit / Loss (Sales Revenue - Cost of Sales)

topics.example: A factory calculating a quotation for a government supply contract uses a Cost Sheet to determine unit production cost and add desired profit margin.
remember: Per-unit cost of production = Total Production Cost / Units Produced; Per-unit selling cost = Total Selling Cost / Units Sold.
mistakes: Dividing selling overheads by units produced instead of units sold.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key advantage of preparing a Cost Sheet?
o: Helps in estimating quotation prices for tenders
quiz.why: A Cost Sheet provides detailed unit cost figures necessary for quoting tender prices.

quiz.q: Per unit selling overhead is calculated by dividing total selling overhead by:
quiz.why: Selling overheads relate directly to goods sold, so the denominator is units sold.
